response.text:
I'll work through each chapter draft systematically, applying the seven tests and gate test to every candidate.

---

**Ch 007 draft candidates:**

1. `"About Gatsby," he corrected himself.` — In the source, Tom says "About Gatsby!" as a clarification after Jordan's joke about a medium. In the draft, this becomes `"About Gatsby," he corrected himself.` — but who is "correcting himself"? In context it reads as Tom, and the antecedent Tom is present in the draft. This parses fine with slight awkwardness. Not a structural failure.

2. `"You must have gone there about the time Biloxi went to New Haven."` — "Biloxi" appears here with no prior establishment in the draft. The Biloxi comic detour is an **authorized removal**. This is a direct residue of that authorized cut. Not a finding.

3. The Wilson/Myrtle garage stop passage: The draft compresses the Wilson exchange and then inserts: `"He was so sick that he looked guilty—unforgivably guilty—as if he had just got some poor girl with child. He had discovered that Myrtle had some sort of life apart from him in another world, and the shock had made him physically sick. Tom, who had made a parallel discovery less than an hour before, paid and stepped on the accelerator."` — This is internally coherent in the draft. No issue.

4. `"Over the ash-heaps the giant eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg kept their vigil, and from the window over the garage Myrtle Wilson peered down, wide-eyed with jealous terror—not at Tom, but at Jordan Baker, whom she took to be his wife."` — Eckleburg's eyes were mentioned earlier in the draft during the approach to Wilson's garage. Jordan Baker is present and named in the draft. This reads fine.

5. The Plaza Hotel compression: `"The room was large and stifling..."` — The draft cuts the explanation of how they ended up there (the "prolonged and tumultuous argument," the "crazy idea" of mint juleps, the baffled clerk). The draft just jumps straight to the room. Does a reader lack a necessary referent? The draft does say `"we all took the less explicable step of engaging the parlour of a suite in the Plaza Hotel"` one paragraph before. The room is established. Fine.

6. `"From the ballroom below came the portentous chords of Mendelssohn's Wedding March, and a long cheer floated in at the window."` — In the source, after the Wedding March passage, Daisy reminisces about her wedding and "Biloxi" is introduced. The draft cuts the Biloxi detour (authorized) and jumps straight to `"We're getting old," said Daisy.` Then: `"Gatsby's foot beat a short, restless tattoo. Tom eyed him suddenly. 'By the way, Mr. Gatsby, I understand you're an Oxford man.'"` This is coherent without Biloxi.

7. `"You must have gone there about the time Biloxi went to New Haven."` — As noted, authorized cut residue.

8. The Jordan phone call in Ch 008: `"You weren't so nice to me last night." "How could it have mattered then?"` — In the source, Nick's line is attributed: `"How could it have mattered then?"` is Nick's reply. In the draft, Jordan's opener `"You weren't so nice to me last night."` is present, and Nick's reply follows. But wait — in the source there is a line before Jordan's opener: `"Probably it had been tactful to leave Daisy's house, but the act annoyed me, and her next remark made me rigid."` The draft cuts this setup. Does the dialogue still parse? Yes — we know Jordan is on the phone. Nick's reply is attributable. Not a structural failure.

9. Ch 008 draft — the Wilson night vigil section. The draft replaces Michaelis with "a neighbor" throughout: `"A neighbor sat with him, first with others, later alone..."` and `"The neighbor made clumsy efforts..."` and `"Standing behind him the neighbor saw..."` — Michaelis is on the **authorized removal list**. The replacement with "the neighbor" descriptor is consistent throughout. Not a finding.

10. Ch 008 draft — `"The chauffeur heard the shots—afterwards he could only say he hadn't thought anything much about them."` — In the source this reads: `"The chauffeur—he was one of Wolfshiem's protégés—heard the shots..."` The draft drops the appositive gloss. Is the chauffeur identifiable? Yes — he was just mentioned two paragraphs before pumping up the mattress. The reader knows who the chauffeur is. Not a finding.

11. Ch 007 draft — `"The afternoon's heat had broken; dusk gathered in the valley of ashes. In the garage office Wilson had locked his wife upstairs and spoke, in a colourless way turned hard and strange, about moving West. Then the racket overhead, the rush of a body through the dark, the cry—'Beat me! Throw me down and beat me, you dirty little coward!'—and the bursting out into the road."` — This is a compressed substitute for the Michaelis section (authorized removal). The passage jumps from Nick's birthday/bridge scene directly to this summary of Wilson locking up Myrtle. The source's Michaelis scene established who is doing what. In the draft, "Wilson had locked his wife upstairs" is introduced without any witness framing (Michaelis's perspective is gone). But "the garage office" — was this established? In the draft chapter, the earlier gas-stop scene established Wilson's garage. "Wilson" is established. "His wife" = Myrtle, established. Does "the colourless way turned hard and strange" parse? It's odd but not broken. The passage functions as a summary transition. A competent reader can parse it. Not a structural failure under the gate test.

12. Ch 007 draft — `"'About Gatsby,' he corrected himself."` — Let me re-examine. In the source:

> "About Gatsby."  
> "About Gatsby! No, I haven't. I said I'd been making a small investigation of his past."

In the draft:
> "Do you mean you've been to a medium?" inquired Jordan humorously.  
> "What?" Confused, he stared at us as we laughed. "A medium?"  
> "About Gatsby," he corrected himself.  
> "And you found he was an Oxford man," said Jordan helpfully.

The source has Jordan saying "About Gatsby" as a clarifying prompt to Tom. Tom then misreads it and says "About Gatsby! No, I haven't." The draft reassigns the line `"About Gatsby"` to Tom as self-correction — which is a compressed but coherent reading. A reader could follow this, though it slightly misrepresents who said what. But is the reader *confused*? The flow is: Jordan asks about medium → Tom confused → "About Gatsby," he corrected himself (i.e., Tom redirects) → Jordan says he found he's an Oxford man. This actually reads as Tom re-clarifying the topic. A competent reader can track it. Not a structural failure.

13. Ch 008 draft — Jordan phone call. The draft begins the call with Jordan's line `"I've left Daisy's house,"` then immediately goes to `"You weren't so nice to me last night."` with no attribution tag. In the source, the sequence is:

> "I've left Daisy's house," she said. [...prose about Nick's reaction...] "You weren't so nice to me last night."

In the draft there is no intervening prose — her second line follows directly after the first. Is the speaker ambiguous? No — it's a continuous phone call with Jordan. Fine.

14. Ch 008 draft — `"It was Jordan Baker; she often called me at this hour because her movements between hotels and clubs and private houses made her hard to find any other way."` — Source has: `"she often called me up at this hour because the uncertainty of her own movements between hotels and clubs and private houses made her hard to find in any other way."` Trimmed but parseable. Fine.

15. Ch 007 — `"We came up with their blue coupé under the spidery girders of the elevated."` — In the source the coupé is described as "easygoing blue coupé." In the draft this is the first time "blue coupé" appears in this portion of the chase. Earlier in the draft, when dividing cars, the draft says Daisy and Gatsby would follow "in the coupé" — but which car is the coupé? In the source and draft, Tom drives Gatsby's big car and the others take Tom's coupé. The draft earlier: `"We'll follow you in the coupé."` Then: `"Jordan and Tom and I got into the front seat of Gatsby's car."` So Daisy and Gatsby are in the (Tom's) coupé. Then `"We came up with their blue coupé"` — this tracks. Fine.

16. Ch 007 draft — `"That was it. I'd never understood before."` — antecedent is "Her voice is full of money." Clear. Fine.

17. Ch 008 draft — the Catherine passage. Source Ch 008 has a passage about Catherine (Myrtle's sister) arriving at the garage. Catherine is on the **authorized removal list**. The draft omits this passage entirely. No residue reference to Catherine in the draft. Fine — nothing to flag.

18. Ch 007 draft, the Walter Chase passage: `"I guess your friend Walter Chase wasn't too proud to come in on it."` — Walter Chase appears without prior introduction in either chapter's draft. Let me check: is Walter Chase a "minor/removable character" on the authorized list? He is NOT on the authorized removal list. He appears in Ch 007 draft without any identifying gloss. However — is he a "minor proper name" requiring a gloss? The source also introduces him without prior setup, in the same scene. Walter Chase is introduced in the source as Gatsby's interlocutor-accusation: `"I guess your friend Walter Chase wasn't too proud to come in on it."` Tom then responds about Chase. The source doesn't gloss him with a role identifier before this either — his role is *established in the dialogue itself* ("he went to jail for a month over in New Jersey," "Wolfshiem scared him into shutting his mouth"). The draft preserves all this context. A reader understands Walter Chase as a mutual criminal associate from the dialogue. Not a structural failure under the gate test.

19. Ch 007 draft — `"I was thirty. Before me stretched the portentous, menacing road of a new decade—thirty—the promise of a decade of loneliness, a thinning list of single men to know, a thinning briefcase of enthusiasm, thinning hair. But there was Jordan beside me, who, unlike Daisy, was too wise ever to carry well-forgotten dreams from age to age. As we passed over the dark bridge her wan face fell lazily against my coat's shoulder and the formidable stroke of thirty died away with the reassuring pressure of her hand."` — This passage in the draft appears to be positioned *before* `"So we drove on toward death through the cooling twilight."` But in the source, this birthday/bridge passage occurs as Nick rides with Tom in the coupé back to Long Island *after* leaving the Plaza, before the crash. In the draft, this passage flows from the Plaza scene directly. Then `"So we drove on toward death"` follows. Then `"The afternoon's heat had broken; dusk gathered in the valley of ashes."` — Does the birthday/Jordan passage in the draft make the reader think Nick is in a different car than he was? No — the draft has Tom, Nick, and Jordan in the coupé. The passage is coherent. Fine.

20. Ch 007 draft — `"The afternoon's heat had broken; dusk gathered in the valley of ashes. In the garage office Wilson had locked his wife upstairs and spoke, in a colourless way turned hard and strange, about moving West."` — This is a mid-scene narrative pivot. The previous paragraph ended: `"So we drove on toward death through the cooling twilight."` The draft then shifts perspective to the garage/Wilson without any framing. In the source, the Michaelis section is a separate narrator insertion, clearly framed. In the draft, without Michaelis, the summary `"In the garage office Wilson had locked his wife upstairs"` appears with no witness identified. But the source's Michaelis framing established who observed this — the draft's compression leaves it as free narration without a clear observer. However, this is a **direct residue of the authorized Michaelis removal**. The authorized subplot/character removals include Michaelis. This seam is expected. Not a finding.

21. Ch 008 draft — `"'I spoke to her,' he muttered after a long silence. 'I told her she might fool me but she couldn't fool God. I took her to the window'—with an effort he got up and pressed his face against the rear pane—'and I said "God knows what you've been doing, everything you've been doing. You may fool me, but you can't fool God!"'"` — `"Standing behind him the neighbor saw that he was looking at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, pale and enormous on the billboard, emerging from the dissolving night."` — Eckleburg's eyes are described as `"pale and enormous on the billboard."` In the Ch 007 draft, the Eckleburg billboard/eyes were established: `"Doctor T. J. Eckleburg's faded eyes came into sight down the road"` and `"Over the ash-heaps the giant eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg kept their vigil."` So the Ch 008 reference is established from the previous draft chapter. Fine.

22. Ch 008 draft — the dog-leash scene. The neighbor finds a dog-leash in the drawer. In the source (Ch 008), this is Michaelis's discovery. The draft has "the neighbor" — consistent with the Michaelis removal. But there's a prior setup: in Ch 002 (source), Tom buys a dog for Myrtle in the apartment. The dog-leash found in Wilson's garage is a different object — it's Myrtle's, suggesting an affair. The draft presents it as: `"There was nothing in it but a small, expensive dog-leash, made of leather and braided silver. It was apparently new."` A reader seeing this in the draft Ch 008 — is the significance clear? The neighbor/Wilson's reaction makes clear it's suspicious. The significance (that someone gave Myrtle a fancy leash as a gift, suggesting another man) comes through from the dialogue. Fine.

23. Now let me carefully check the **Jordan phone call in Ch 008 draft** for unattributed dialogue:

Source:
> "Probably it had been tactful to leave Daisy's house, but the act annoyed me, and her next remark made me rigid."  
> "You weren't so nice to me last night."  
> "How could it have mattered then?"

Draft:
> "I've left Daisy's house," she said. "I'm at Hempstead, and I'm going down to Southampton this afternoon."  
> "You weren't so nice to me last night."  
> "How could it have mattered then?"

There is no speaker tag on `"You weren't so nice to me last night."` — but it's clearly Jordan continuing. And Nick's reply is untagged too but clearly Nick. In a phone dialogue, the two-voice structure is clear. Not a structural failure.

24. Ch 007 draft — checking for any mid-scene jump at the chapter opening. The chapter 7 draft opens with the Trimalchio passage. Chapter 6 draft (not shown here) would need to have established Gatsby's parties/career. The opening references "his career as Trimalchio" — this is a self-contained phrase (it says "his career as Trimalchio was over"). A reader who hasn't seen Ch 006 still gets that Gatsby's party-hosting phase has ended. This is coherent.

25. Ch 008 draft — `"Up in the city, I tried to list the quotations on an interminable amount of stock, then fell asleep in my swivel-chair."` — This references Nick's work life in the city. Ch 003 authorized cut removes "Nick's New York work life." However, this sentence doesn't introduce anything that requires prior establishment — it's simply Nick at work in the city (which the reader knows from Ch 001). Fine.

26. Ch 008 — `"I called Gatsby's house a few minutes later, but the line was busy. Four times I tried; finally an exasperated central told me the wire was being kept open for long distance from Detroit."` — "central" = telephone operator, a period term. The source uses the same word. A competent reader can infer this from context. Not a gloss failure.

27. Ch 007 draft — checking the "My Finn" reference: `"My Finn informed me that Gatsby had dismissed every servant..."` — "My Finn" appears without any prior introduction in the Ch 007 draft. This is a minor character — Nick's Finnish housekeeper/servant. She does not appear anywhere earlier in the Ch 007 draft, nor has she been established in Ch 006 (the preceding chapter, whose draft I don't have but can reason about — in the source, "My Finn" appears in Ch 007 for the first time). In the source, "My Finn" is also introduced here without prior setup — it's a casual possessive that establishes her as Nick's domestic worker. The phrase "My Finn" functions as a descriptor (Nick's Finnish servant). Under the rules: *"A minor character is referred to only by a descriptor... and the descriptor is clear; proper-name continuity is not required when the name has been elided."* "My Finn" is a descriptor, not a proper name. And the role is clear from the possessive "My" — Nick's household helper. **Not a finding.**

28. Ch 007 draft — `"He was calling at Daisy's request—would I come to lunch at her house tomorrow? Half an hour later Daisy herself telephoned and seemed relieved to find that I was coming."` — The source has: `"He was calling up at Daisy's request—would I come to lunch at her house tomorrow? Miss Baker would be there."` The draft cuts `"Miss Baker would be there."` This is a minor trimming. The draft sentence still parses. Fine.

29. Ch 008 draft — Wilson's movements: `"His movements—on foot all the time—were afterward traced to Port Roosevelt and then to Gad's Hill, where he bought a sandwich he didn't eat and a cup of coffee."` — "Port Roosevelt" and "Gad's Hill" are place names that appear without gloss. Are these "minor proper names" requiring identification? The rule applies to *characters*, not place names. And even as place names, their role is clear from context (locations Wilson passed through). Not a finding.

30. Now, carefully: Ch 008 draft — `"Until long after midnight a changing crowd lapped up against the front of the garage, while George Wilson rocked himself back and forth on a couch inside."` — The source has this with Michaelis explicitly as observer/companion. The draft drops Michaelis (authorized) and replaces with "A neighbor sat with him." But then the dog-leash scene: in the source, Michaelis opens the drawer. In the draft: `"Wilson pointed suddenly. 'Look in the drawer there,' he said. 'Which drawer?' 'That drawer—that one.' There was nothing in it but a small, expensive dog-leash..."` — The neighbor is implied to be the one responding and discovering the leash. The exchange `"This?" the neighbor asked, holding it up.` — who is "the neighbor"? This is consistent with the "neighbor" established two paragraphs before. Coherent.

31. Ch 007 draft — `"'About Gatsby,' he corrected himself."` — I want to reconsider this one. In the source:

> "Do you mean you've been to a medium?" inquired Jordan humorously.  
> "What?" Confused, he stared at us as we laughed. "A medium?"  
> **"About Gatsby."**  
> "About Gatsby! No, I haven't. I said I'd been making a small investigation of his past."

In the source, `"About Gatsby."` is **Jordan's** line — she's redirecting/clarifying what she meant. Tom then responds `"About Gatsby! No, I haven't."` 

In the draft:
> "Do you mean you've been to a medium?" inquired Jordan humorously.  
> "What?" Confused, he stared at us as we laughed. "A medium?"  
> **"About Gatsby," he corrected himself.**  
> "And you found he was an Oxford man," said Jordan helpfully.

The draft reassigns Jordan's clarifying line to Tom, attributed with "he corrected himself." This is a compression that changes who speaks. The result: Tom says "A medium?" then immediately "About Gatsby" as self-correction — meaning Tom is clarifying what he was investigating. Then Jordan says "And you found he was an Oxford man." 

Does this *confuse* a reader? The dialogue sequence is: Jordan jokes about medium → Tom confused → Tom self-corrects to the topic (Gatsby) → Jordan follows up. This actually reads coherently as Tom redirecting. A reader won't be lost. The meaning is slightly altered (it was Jordan who prompted "about Gatsby" in the source) but the draft version parses cleanly. **Gate test: reader is reading a compressed version, not confused.** Not a finding.

32. Let me check one more potential issue: Ch 007 draft — `"The next day was broiling... The straw seats of the car hovered on the edge of combustion; the conductor's hand left a dark stain on my commutation ticket."` The source has an extended heat description including a woman fainting/dropping her pocketbook and the conductor speaking. The draft cuts this and compresses to `"the conductor's hand left a dark stain on my commutation ticket."` This is a standalone descriptive sentence that doesn't require prior establishment. Fine.

33. Ch 007 draft — `"Through the hall of the Buchanans' house blew a faint wind, carrying the sound of the telephone bell out to Gatsby and me as we waited at the door. The butler glistened and bade us into the salon—as though in this heat every extra gesture were an affront to the common store of life."` — The source has the butler's comic exchange ("The master's body?") which is cut. The draft's compressed version attributes the "affront" thought to the butler's gesturing. This is slightly reattributed but parseable. Fine.

34. Ch 007 draft — `"Jordan's fingers, powdered white over their tan, rested for a moment in mine. Simultaneously I heard Tom's voice, gruff and husky, at the hall telephone."` — Source has: `"'And Mr. Thomas Buchanan, the athlete?' I inquired. Simultaneously I heard his voice..."` The draft cuts Nick's inquiry about Tom (and Tom's full name/athlete gloss). The source's gloss "the athlete" is descriptive irony, but Tom is a continuously present major character. Not a minor-name gloss issue. Fine.

35. Final check — Ch 008 draft, the Eckleburg theological moment: `"Standing behind him the neighbor saw that he was looking at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, pale and enormous on the billboard, emerging from the dissolving night."` The source: `"Michaelis saw with a shock that he was looking at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, which had just emerged, pale and enormous, from the dissolving night."` The source says `"which had just emerged"` — the billboard eyes "emerging from" the dissolving night as the dawn comes up. The draft says `"pale and enormous on the billboard, emerging from the dissolving night"` — adding "on the billboard" which is a gloss not in the source. This is actually slightly better for a reader. Fine.

After this exhaustive review, I find **no valid structural coherence failures** in either draft. The compression has been careful: authorized removals are clean, major characters are tracked, dialogue exchanges are attributable, and the gate test confirms that a competent reader would be reading a less-ornamented but structurally sound abridgment throughout.
